title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Method for Bank Account Fraud Detection using Quantum Encoding and Quantum Machine Learning
journal_or_venue: 2024 IEEE MIT Undergraduate Research Technology Conference (URTC)
abstract_summary: The paper proposes a hybrid quantum-classical approach to bank account fraud detection and introduces a novel classification called Devastating Evolutionary Dynamic Entities (DEDE) to characterize evolving fraud threats. Due to current NISQ hardware limits the authors use a hybrid setup (classical preprocessing and quantum models) and find classical XGBoost outperforms the quantum-support approach, though the quantum method shows moderate performance on limited samples and highlights potential for future improvements as quantum hardware matures.
methodology_description: The study compared a classical state-of-the-art fraud detection pipeline (XGBoost) against a hybrid quantum-classical approach using a quantum-kernel SVM (QSVM). The authors used the Feedzai Research synthetic bank-account fraud suite (six temporal variants) as the data source. For the classical pipeline minimal preprocessing was applied (duplicates and highly correlated features removed, categorical level-encoding where required), an 80/20 train/test split was used, and XGBoost hyperparameters were tuned via RandomSearchCV (150 iterations, 3-fold CV) over parameters including step size (eta), gamma and max_depth. For the quantum pipeline heavier preprocessing was required: columns with >25% missing values were dropped, rows with remaining missing values were removed, categorical features level-encoded, and numerical features scaled. Due to hardware/time constraints the feature set was reduced so that 8 features were encoded into 8 qubits (authors initially intended 16). The quantum encoding used Angle Encoding to build a quantum circuit/kernel; a quantum kernel was constructed and passed to an SVM classifier (QSVM). The quantum experiments were trained on 750 instances (250 fraud, 500 non-fraud) with a matching 750-instance test set; each quantum run was repeated six times and the quantum kernel was re-run for each dataset variant. Evaluation across methods used standard classification metrics (precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, accuracy) and comparison against the classical XGBoost baseline.
algorithms_used: Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM) / SVM with quantum kernel
experimental_setup: Hybrid quantum-classical approach on NISQ-era hardware/resources; due to hardware/time constraints the quantum experiments were restricted to 8 qubits (intended 16) and small sample sizes. No specific QPU or simulator was reported.
dataset_used: Feedzai Research synthetic bank account fraud suite (six temporal variants, Feb–Sep). Each variant contains 31 features and over 1 million instances; data include induced Laplacian noise and injected biases (group-size, prevalence, temporal) to mimic real-world conditions.
experiment_input: Source: Feedzai Research synthetic bank-account fraud datasets (6 temporal variants). Size: each variant >1M instances, 31 features. Preprocessing (classical): removed duplicates, removed highly correlated features, level-encoded categorical variables, 80/20 train-test split. Preprocessing (quantum): dropped columns with >25% missing values, removed rows with remaining missing values, level-encoded categorical features, feature scaling, reduced feature set to 8 features for 8 qubits. Quantum sampling: training set 750 instances (250 fraud / 500 non-fraud), test set 750 instances.
experiment_process: Classical pipeline: basic cleaning (duplicates/correlation removal), encoding, 80/20 split, XGBoost training with RandomSearchCV hyperparameter tuning (150 iterations, 3-fold CV) over parameters such as eta, gamma, max_depth; evaluation via precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, accuracy. Quantum pipeline: aggressive cleaning to remove missingness, level-encoding categorical variables, scaling; select 8 features (one per qubit), apply Angle Encoding to build quantum circuit and quantum kernel; train SVM using the quantum kernel (QSVM) on 750-sample training set, test on 750-sample test set; each experiment repeated six times and kernel re-computed per dataset variant. No circuit depths, shot counts, optimizer details or explicit kernel hyperparameters were reported.
experiment_output: Reported metrics: precision, recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC, and accuracy per dataset variant. Baseline: classical XGBoost achieved high ROC-AUC (approximately 89%–95%) and strong F1/precision/recall. Quantum QSVM produced lower KPI scores relative to the classical baseline; results presented comparatively across the six dataset variants with qualitative discussion about bias effects and hardware/sample limitations.

[supported] The hybrid quantum-classical QSVM (angle encoding) that the authors implemented, using 8 qubits and small sample sizes, underperformed the classical XGBoost baseline in this study.

[supported] Quantum experiments were materially constrained by current NISQ hardware and practical limits: the authors reduced features to 8 qubits, removed features/rows with missing values, and trained on 750 instances (250 fraud, 500 non-fraud) for the QSVM.

[supported] The Feedzai dataset suite used contains six temporal variants, each with ~31 features and over 1 million instances, and incorporates induced Laplacian noise, missing values, and designed biases to mimic real-world conditions.

[supported] The authors found that NISQ-era limitations (noise, qubit count, computational overhead) and small sample sizes meaningfully degrade quantum/hybrid model KPI scores relative to classical models.

results_summary: The paper compares a state-of-the-art classical fraud detector (XGBoost) with a hybrid quantum-classical QSVM on Feedzai synthetic bank-account fraud datasets. XGBoost, tuned via RandomSearchCV, achieved high ROC-AUC (reported ~89%–95%), while the implemented hybrid QSVM (angle encoding, 8 qubits, trained on 750 samples) underperformed the classical baseline. The authors attribute the quantum model's lower KPIs to NISQ hardware limitations, limited feature/qubit counts, small training samples, and the need to remove features/rows with missing data. They conclude that hybrid quantum-classical methods do not outperform classical methods under current hardware constraints, but consider quantum approaches promising for the future.

key_ideas: #idea:hybrid-approach — Proposes a hybrid pipeline: classical preprocessing + quantum-kernel SVM (QSVM) with Angle Encoding for bank account fraud detection.
#idea:near-term-feasibility — Empirical evaluation on limited NISQ-era resources shows QSVM is feasible at small scale but not yet competitive with classical methods.
#limitation:qubit-count — Intended 16-feature encoding was reduced to 8 qubits due to hardware/time constraints, constraining model expressivity.
#limitation:noise — Authors attribute degraded quantum model KPIs to NISQ-era limitations (noise and hardware constraints).

#limitation:data-encoding — Heavy preprocessing and feature reduction were required to encode classical features into an 8-qubit angle-encoded kernel (high encoding overhead); key circuit parameters (shots, depth, optimizer) are unreported.
#limitation:simulation-only — No specific QPU or simulator is reported, reducing reproducibility and making it unclear whether results reflect real-hardware behaviour.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Classical XGBoost (with hyperparameter tuning) substantially outperformed the QSVM baseline on the Feedzai synthetic fraud datasets (ROC-AUC ~89–95% for XGBoost vs lower for QSVM).

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Small training/test sizes (750 each) and repeated runs show moderate QSVM performance but limited statistical power; authors frame results as indicative rather than conclusive.
contradictions: This paper finds classical XGBoost outperforms a QSVM on realistic synthetic fraud datasets, contradicting optimistic claims that current quantum-ML approaches already surpass classical baselines.
The need to reduce features from 16 to 8 qubits and train on very small samples contradicts claims that NISQ-era quantum methods can scale to production-sized financial datasets.
